Introduction - April 2010 











##### **Introduction** 

- **_Our preferred economic indicator the OECD Composite Leading Indicator continues to point in the right direction for a broad-based recovery in base metals demand.   It rose to 103.6 in February from a downwardly revised 102.9.  Growth was seen in G-7 category (103.7 from 103.0).  The major Asia 5 category increased from 102.8 to 102.6._** 

- **_The near term tightness in the aluminium market, brought about by a significant amount of material being tied up in long-term fin

ancing deals, has remained a supportive factor to prices. However, given the massive oversupply GFMS believe that the market is vulnerable to a correction and consequently expect aluminium to underperform the rest of the sector in 2010._** - **_Copper consumption is starting to improve and there are signs that some consumer restocking is taking place. Furthermore, the recent tragic events in Chile highlight the uncertain and volatile nature of copper supply. Whilst the fundamentals do remain by and large weak, they have been improving and this has been reflected by falls in both LME and SHFE inventories in recent weeks._** - **_In the lead market, demand from the replacement battery sector provided less support than might have been anticipated over the first quarter when taking into account the severity of the winter weather. Partly as a result of this, lead underperformed considerably in relation to the rest of the base metals complex over Q1._** ###### **~~Base Metals & Other Commodity Prices~~** 250

With our index giving equal weighting to each metal, the GFMS base metal index largely reflects the particularly strong performance of the nickel market over the month. March and the second quarter is always a strong period for demand from a seasonal perspective. There are some signs that base metal demand is beginning to finally respond to the improvement in the mature economies, which has long been flagged by the forward-looking indicators such as the various purchasing managers’ surveys that we track and the OECD composite leading indicator. ###### **~~Base Metals Prices in Major Currencies~~** 250

Introduction - April 2010 











Our general view on the base metal markets is that 2010 will prove to be a year of consolidation after the exceptional gains seen in 2009.  The key remains the extent to which the current upward momentum provided by investors can be maintained.  Liquidations, brought about by metal-specific news and macroeconomic developments, are likely to lead to periods of price weakness.  However, similarly to the rebound from the early-February lows, such dips are likely to be viewed as buying opportunities by bargain-hunting investors and also consumers. 

Such macroeconomic developments over the short term include the uncertain direction of the economies of the US and Europe, and whether the early signs of improvement in some key indicators can be maintained.  In this regard, we recognise the somewhat fragile nature of the recovery within the mature economies and the fact that the acceleration 

in growth will be relatively modest compared to previous cyclical recoveries. 

Having said this, we are reasonably optimistic about the demand prospects for the base metals markets over the second half of the year.  A key reason for this is that downstream inventories at fabricators have been kept low during this cycle.  Consequently, once fabricators begin to see signs of an improvement in underlying demand, the base metals markets should receive a boost in the form of restocking. 

Furthermore we believe that, despite concerns over monetary tightening measures, China will remain a key driver of growth which will provide significant support to the sector over the year.

However many headwinds remain, which are only showing gradual signs of improvement. The ISM index in the US continued to show expansion in March, increasing by 3.1 points to 59.6, which took the index to its highest level since 2004. This outperformed expectations and was reflective of increases in new orders and production in addition to strong growth in inventories, indicating that there may finally be a degree of restocking taking place. In contrast, after strong growth last month, the employment index dipped slightly on the month to 55.1, from 56.1 in February. Overall, the March survey is consistent with gains in industrial production. These conditions were reflected by the Conference Board Index of consumer confidence, which picked up to 52.5 from an upwardly revised 46.4 in February. However, this fol

e’s debt, despite Eurozone leaders agreeing on a bailout package, will continue to overhang sentiment in the region. For the first quarter conditions remained lacklustre, highlighted by the fact that German industrial production saw little pick up over the first two months of the year. This was likely affected by the abnormally cold winter weather and the phasing out of some scrappage schemes that provided a temporary reprieve in the auto market towards the end of last year. Indeed, after stagnating in the fourth quarter of 2009, we believe that German GDP growth remained subdued over the first quarter, a trend which is likely to have taken place across much of the Eurozone. The labour market continues to be a significant area of concern for the global economic recovery. In the US, hiring remains low although layoffs have showed signs of easing up. In line with this, and also reflective of the lack of credit availability, new home sales fell once again in February, to a record low of 308,000 units on an annualised basis. Although we may see some support from the extended tax credit, the housing market will remain subdued. In Japan, the Tankan survey showed improving business sentiment over the first quarter, although the country is heavily reliant on continued strength in Chinese demand. With the country mired in deflation, as weak domestic demand continues to weigh on prices, GFMS believe that Japan is set for a difficult year over 2010. Independent - Informed - International **E2** Copper - April 2010 ##### **Copper** ###### **Recent developments** - **_Copper cash prices continued their rebound from the early February lows in impressive style, rising to a high of $7,951/tonne on April 6th. The rise reflects the positive view of investors towards copper on an improving economic outlook and was also supported by a degree of restocking._** - **_Supportive of this, LME stocks declined over the month and currently reside around 510,000 tonnes. However, after seeing a decline late in March, stocks on the Shanghai Futures Exchange picked up again in early April to over 169,500 tonnes._** - **_Chinese demand continues to support the global total, with February imports rebounding from the low total seen in the previous month._** - **_Although generally picking up from lows, demand in the mature economies remains muted. This is highlighted by recent data on the key construction industry._** - **_For this year as a whole, GFMS believes that the copper will average $7,485/tonne as consumption is expected to rise and investor interest is likely to remain strong. The supply situation is also tight and should demand pick up faster than expected or there be supply disruptions, then the market could quickly become noticeably tight._** - **_Given our expectations for growth and with stocks having built up in recent years, a return to the record high price in 2008 are unlikely to be seen until stocks have started to trend lower._** - **_There is, however, considerable downside potential within the copper market. This reflects a number of factors. Most importantly, prices are currently nearly double average costs of production, and also above marginal costs. From the demand side, the recovery in offtake outside of China has been slow to emerge. In addition, given the exceptional gains in the copper price over the last year, we could see liquidation from the funds on any signs of fundamental weakness._** ###### **Outlook for the next 12 months** ###### **~~GFMS’ Forecast Scenarios~~** - **_In line with a renewed optimism about the prospects for economic recovery, prices continued the strong rebound seen last month. However, given the continued uncertainty over the global economic outlook, GFMS believe that the market will drop back from the recent highs. Thereafter, we believe that Q2 will generally be a period of consolidation for the base metals as the market evaluates the extent of the economic recovery._** |**~~Copper Supply-D~~**

Independent - Informed - International **C1** Copper - April 2010 ###### **Market Background** Having dipped by 7.3% in February to $6,848/tonne on Greece’s debt woes and wide-spread sale of “risky” assets, prices re-gained momentum in March to reach the highest monthly average since August 2008 of $7,463/tonne. While the cash price spent much of the month hovering around $7,400/tonne, the last few days saw it climb, to end the month and the quarter on $7,830/tonne. Copper’s rally however came to a halt on April 6th by which time the spot price had reached a one and a half year high of $7,951/tonne. This, in part, reflects the positive view of investors towards copper and by the unfortunate events that took place in Chile in late February and their perceived implications on copper mine production in the country. Although copper’s immediate fundamentals remain by and large weak, we certainly believe that copper’s recent rally is a reflection of some consumer restocking, which has been taking place against a backdrop of an improving global economy. ###### **Recovery in mature economies remains muted** Within the ICSG’s total, unsurprisingly, the more advanced economies experienced the largest declines. Consumption in the United States and Europe fell by an estimated 19% while in Japan demand for copper dropped by 26%. Indeed, the various indicators relating to their key end use markets show that, although generally picking up from lows, the recovery over the second half of the year was painfully slow in these markets. Although we expect them to improve as 2010 progresses, key end use data pertaining to the individual markets suggest that the recovery so far remains muted. In February, US housing starts fell by almost 6.0% m-o-m to 575,000 tonnes. On a positive note however, they held up better than expected given the magnitude of the winter storms. The outlook calls for a steady improvement over the next few quarters, but the support the economy w

ill receive from housing starts this year will be modest, at best. Falling inventories certainly confirm our view. LME stocks have declined by 8.0% from the recent high of 555,075 tonnes in mid-February to around 510,000 tonnes. Similarly, deliverable copper stocks in warehouses monitored by the Shanghai Futures Exchange have also been slipping in recent weeks. At 153,589 tonnes, they are down by 9.2% from levels of 169,101 tonnes in mid-late March. The situation in Europe is similar. The construction sector remains weak especially in northern Europe after a severe winter which put on hold many construction projects. KME recently announced that its output of copper, alloy and special products fell by 23% to 437,000 tonnes in 2009; however a trend expected to reverse this year. According to the company, output should have risen by 10-12% in the first quarter of the year. ###### **Demand growth remains weak** Having seen negative growth of 0.9% in 2008, the latest batch of data by the International Copper Study Group (ICSG) suggests a drop of 0.1% to 17.988 million tonnes. Although demand remained subdued for most of the year, an upward trend has been apparent since the start of the fourth quarter. GFMS believe that the decline in 2009 was greater at 1.7% as we highlight in the GFMS Copper Survey. For further information on the 2009 Copper Survey please contact info@gfms.co.uk. By comparison, housing starts in Japan not only fell by 13.0% m-o-m but also contracted by 9.3% year-on-year to 56,527 units in February. The monthly decline comes after several months of strong growth, fuelled mainly by rising government construction. Preliminary statistics by the Japan Copper and Brass Association however suggest that the country produced 68,781 tonnes of rolled copper products in February, almost double the amount from a year earlier, nevertheless down 3.4% from the previous month. ###### **Chinese production increases from a low base** 

According to the CNI-A, Chinese refined copper output came in at 714,459 tonnes in the opening two months of the year, up by 17.2% year-on-year.  Within this, Antaike estimates that China’s 13 main copper producers produced 546,400 tonnes of copper and that operating rates were 80% in the month.  Indeed, there was enough concentrate available to support this growth.  The organisation estimates that output of copper in concentrate increased by 32.5% over the same period to 146,240 tonnes, albeit from a low base. 

One of the main concerns regarding Chinese demand going forward is the uncertainty over the level of unreported inventories within the country.  During our recent field research visits to China, we believe that the level of stocks is at the bottom end of the much quoted 500,000-1,300,000 tonne range (this issue is discussed in detail in the 2010 Copper Survey). 

###### **ICSG, market surplus expands in 2009** 

According to the ICSG, the copper market registered a surplus of 365,000 tonnes last year most of which took place in the first half of the year.  However, we estimate that the market experienced a surplus of 777,000 tonnes.  This has been discussed in great depth in our inaugural 2009 Copper Survey.  The ICSG’s estimate compares with a smaller surplus of 224,000 tonnes in 2008. 

###### **…supported by relatively high imports** 

Having started the New Year on a weak note, Chinese imports of refined copper picked up by 12.2% m-o-m in February, which took the year-to-date total to 417,869 tonnes.  It comes as little surprise that they were down year-on-year, in fact it was somewhat expected, because of China’s huge purchases last year on the back of low LME prices. 

The organisation continues to point to a tight concentrate market, estimating that global mine production increased by just 1.3% to 15.734 million tonnes.  Importantly, the bulk of the gain came from SX-EW output, which grew by 5.6% year-on-year.  Mine capacity utilisation rates however came in 2.8% lower at 80.6%, which marks the fifth consecutive yearly fall. 

###### **Copper scrap imports set to fall in a new customs rule** 

Chinese imports of copper scrap came in at 277,000 tonnes, down by 17.8% m-o-m from 337,000 tonnes in January. Recent reports suggest that copper scrap shipments to China may fall in April as a new customs rule to fight duty evasion came into effect at the start of April.  This requires importers

Independent - Informed - International **C3** Copper - April 2010 ###### **Codelco notes a rise in production after years of slippages** After four years of dwindling output, Codelco saw its production of copper rise by 16% to 1.7 million tonnes last year. With the exception of Andina, all of Codelco’s other mines saw year-on-year increases with Gaby noting the largest increase, of 118%. Independent - Informed - International **N1** Nickel & Cobalt - April 2010 ###### **Market Background** The main feature of the nickel market over the course of the first quarter had been its extreme volatility. Nickel spent much of January straddling $18,500/tonne, before slipping to $17,035/tonne in early February. This was, however, followed by a period of strengthening seemingly on the back of news that the 60,000 tonnes per year Goro project has been further delayed. This saw the cash quote rally to $22,875/tonne in early March. Stronger demand conditions (and renewed investment activity) then pushed prices towards $25,000/tonne. Nickel is the best performer among the LME metals with year-to-date gains of around 35%. This is indeed a reflection of the metal’s improving fundamentals, while to a lesser extent fund buying which, of course, has been the key driver behind prices in recent times. Fall

ing LME inventories have undoubtedly been a contributing factor behind nickel’s rally, which after having ballooned last year, and peaked to an all-time high of 166,476 tonnes in early February, have declined to around 156,000 tonnes.  Although the dips have not been huge on a daily basis, we have certainly seen a consistent drawdown, reflecting the strong demand by stainless producers. 

###### **…a trend that GFMS believe should continue going forward** 

Having been weakened by the recent downturn, the European flat rolled stainless market has certainly showed signs of improvement in the three months to March, characterised by improving demand, tight supply, rising base prices and lengthening lead-times. Second quarter order books are also filling up, with mill deliveries now late May or June.  Most of the current buying activity is coming from distributors, as they seek to rebuild stock levels from previous lows and book material in anticipation of further increases in transaction prices as alloy surcharges continue upwards. End-users are also believed to be rebuilding inventories that should further boost demand. 

The Asian market has also been noting improvements, reflected by increases in domestic prices for 304 grades supported by the rally in the nickel price.  In South Korea, Posco lifted the price of its austenitic coils by $265/tonne for April deliveries, while China’s largest stainless steel producer, Shanxi Taigang, raised its price by $73/tonne.  Taiwanese stainless mills are due to announce their April prices, which we believe will also increase. 

###### **Producers’ dependence on austenitic products falls** 

###### 

The International Stainless Steel Forum (ISSF) has recently published its preliminary 2009 estimates for stainless steel production.  According to the organisation, global stainless output fell by 5.2% to 24.579 million tonnes, following the 6.8% drop in 2008.  Within this, only China experienced positive growth (+26.8%).  Central and Eastern Europe and Western Europe/Africa noted declines in excess of 20%, reflecting the uneven nature of the global economic downturn which saw these two regions more affected than the others.  Similarly, the Americas and Asia (excluding China) recovered faster from the downturn than others, which saw their output fall by relatively less; 15.4% and 11.6%, respectively. 

The collapse in the nickel price early last year saw stainless producers increase their use of nickel, which saw the austenitic ratio nudge upwards in the first half of the year to 61.9%.  Despite this, real nickel demand remained weak. Nevertheless, as prices picked up in the third quarter and consolidated in the fourth, the market share of the 300 series dipped to 60.7% and 58.5%, respectively, which compares with a typical austenitic ratio of between 65-70%. 

Notably, the market share of the 400 series has been growing at its expense.  According to the ISSF, this has increased from 25.2% in the first quarter to

31.1% in the final quarter. The share of 200 series stainless grade however remained on a downward trend throughout 2009. Nickel Premiums

A pickup in “Western World” demand is already apparent as European premiums for nickel briquettes, for example, have increased to $350-400/tonne over the LME nickel price from $200-250/tonne previously. Stocks of drummed nickel briquettes in LME warehouses have dropped by 44% since February 5th to about 2,500 tonnes, which helps explain the increase in the premium. Before, it was really only the United States that was having real supply issues, but now it seems that things have also tightened up over in Europe. ###### **China helps global demand regain positive growth** The latest data provided by the China Non-ferrous Metals Industrial Association (CNI-A) suggests that the country imported 12,200 tonnes of nickel in February, down by 3.5% year-on-year. The year-to-date figure of 28,400 tonnes however was up by some 40.13%. At around this time last year, investors started taking advantage of the low nickel prices by importing record amounts, however this is clearly not the case this year as prices have picked up. As a result, we believe Chinese imports will decline further in March. ###### **Chinese nickel output records a second monthly dip in** ###### **February…** According to the CNI-A, Chinese refined output fell by 9.1% year-on-year in February to 11,900 tonnes, which represents the second consecutive slippage after having reached a record high of 17,089 tonnes in December 2009. The country saw growth of almost 30% last year, supported by consistent monthly production at Jinchuan. In a recent statement, the company has announced its plans to produce 130,000 tonnes this year too. ###### **…however nickel pig iron production in China is picking up** Looking ahead, Chinese nickel pig iron production is set to become a far greater influence on the market than it has been in previous year particularly given the improvement in quality. The bulk of the ore used to produce nickel through this source was imported from Indonesia. According to the CNI-A, China imported 2.1 million tonnes of nickel ore and concentrate over the first two months of the year, 88% more than the same period last year. ###### **2010 productio

Katanga Mining is looking to boost production of cobalt at its operations in the Democratic Republic of Congo to 8,000 tonnes per year in the second quarter of 2011, up from the 5,500 tonne level expected for this year. Furthermore, the Ruashi mine in the DRC produced 812 tonnes of cobalt in the fourth quarter of 2009. During the last six months of last year, cobalt output rose to 1,502 tonnes, from 135 over the same period a year earlier. Also in the DRC, the Big Hill cobalt smelter is scheduled to come back on line in May after a two month closure for maintenance work. Cobalt production has been on a declining trend since peaking in 2007 and 2008 at 5,500 tonnes. After a 9% fall in 2009, to 5,000 tonnes, the smelter is set for another decline this year. ###### **Market outlook** higher than the actual average of $21.8/lb, there are signs that prices are mounting a recovery. Consequently, we see little reason to change our price forecasts for the remainder of the year. GFMS expect a rebound in demand to result in the market seeing a deficit in the first half of 2010, with high grade prices averaging $25 and $26/lb over Q2 and Q3 respectively. However, towards the end of the year may return the market to surplus with a Q4 average of $21/lb. In terms of alternative scenarios, the introduction of trading on the LME should provide a boost given the influence of funds elsewhere in base metals sector. Also there are big question marks concerning the timing about the new projects that are coming on-stream, both the HPAL projects and those in the African cobalt-belt. Under a high case scenario, prices could average $30/lb in the final quarter of 2010. The downside should be fairly limited given that stocks are currently low. On a quarterly average basis, GFMS does not expect prices to fall below $17/lb. As noted in our last report, we expected a rebound in cobalt prices which did materialise over March.
